conceptTag: A restaurant kitchen at rush hour
readerTitle: Why the kitchen gets slower when everyone works harder
caseNote: 가상 사례 (식당 주방, 배관 수리 업체, 소프트웨어 도입 컨설팅사) · 대기 시간 곡선은 표준 대기행렬 이론(M/M/1) 공식으로 계산한 상대값
insight: 러시아워 주방의 지연은 게으름이 아니라 큰 묶음과 여유 없는 가동률에서 나온다. 같은 두 가지 원리가 서비스 사업의 대기 시간도 결정한다.
misconception: 모두가 쉬지 않고 일하고 한 번에 많이 처리할수록 고객이 빨리 받는다.

sources.text: 표준 대기행렬 이론 (M/M/1 모델): 평균 대기 시간은 가동률 u에 대해 u/(1−u)에 비례
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 주방, 배관 업체, 컨설팅사 사례는 모두 가상입니다. 실제 업계 통계나 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why the kitchen gets slower when everyone works harder
body: Friday, 7:30 pm. Every cook is moving fast. Nobody is standing still. Tickets hang in a long row above the pass.
Yet food is reaching tables more slowly than at 6 pm, when the kitchen felt half asleep. Two ideas from this unit explain why, and both apply far outside restaurants.

image.label: Busy kitchen line with a long row of order tickets
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 저녁 러시의 식당 주방. 요리사 세 명이 모두 바쁘게 움직이고, 주문 티켓이 길게 줄지어 걸려 있음. 벽시계는 7:30. 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: The grill cook wants to save time.
body: Burger orders arrive every minute or two. Your grill cook suggests waiting until 12 orders pile up, then cooking them all at once. "Fewer trips, less wasted motion."
What do you tell them?

options.text: Good idea. Cook in batches of 12
options.feedback: You save a few steps, but the first table waits for eleven more orders before its burger even starts. That's **batch size** at work: big batches add waiting.

options.text: Cook in small batches of two or three as orders arrive
options.feedback: Each table waits only for a couple of orders, and a mistake spoils three burgers, not twelve. Small batches keep food moving.

options.text: Batch only during the rush, when it's busiest
options.feedback: Tempting, but the rush is exactly when long waits hurt most. Big batches stretch the line at the worst moment.

cards.title: Big batches make everyone wait for the last order.
body: In a batch of 12, the first burger sits on the board until the twelfth ticket arrives. Fries for that table go cold. The server hovers at the pass.
This is **batch size**, from earlier in the unit: the more you group work together, the longer each item waits for the others.
Batching feels efficient because the cook moves less. But the customer doesn't care about the cook's steps. They care about when their plate arrives.

cards.title: At 6 pm, one cook stands around.
body: Your owner notices that one of three line cooks is idle for long stretches early in the evening. She wants to cut that shift and keep the kitchen "fully used."
What's your advice?

options.text: Cut the shift. Idle time is wasted wages
options.feedback: You save one wage, but two cooks at near full load can't absorb a rush of tables. That's **the utilization trap**: the busier the line, the faster waits explode.

options.text: Keep the cook. Give them prep work they can drop when tickets spike
options.feedback: You get useful work from quiet minutes and keep spare capacity for the rush. Slack that can switch over is the cheapest buffer.

options.text: Keep the cook, but schedule prep so they're never idle
options.feedback: Busy on paper, but if their prep can't wait, they're not free when the 7:30 rush hits. The spare capacity disappears.

cards.title: Waits don't grow evenly. They explode.
body: In a simple model of a busy line, average waiting time rises slowly at first, then sharply as the line nears 100% busy.
Going from 80% to 95% busy doesn't add a little wait. It makes the wait almost **five times** longer.

groups.label: Relative wait time by how busy the line is

cards.callout: That idle cook at 6 pm is what keeps 7:30 from falling apart.

cards.title: A plumber's Friday quotes.
body: A plumbing company writes all its job quotes on Friday afternoons. It feels tidy: one block of desk time a week.

But a customer who calls on Monday waits four days for a price. Many call a rival in the meantime. Switching to quotes within a day, a batch size of one, wins jobs the company was losing without noticing.
Same lesson as the grill: grouping work saves the business effort and costs the customer time.

image.label: Stack of quotes waiting until Friday versus quotes sent same day
image.brief: 좌우 비교 일러스트. 왼쪽: 달력의 금요일 칸에 견적서가 높이 쌓여 있고 고객들이 기다림. 오른쪽: 견적서가 매일 한 장씩 바로 고객에게 날아감. 실제 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: Small batches and slack both have costs.
body: Some work has a real setup cost. Heating an oven for bread or setting up a machine can make larger batches sensible. Shrink batches where setup is cheap first.

Slack costs money too. You don't need spare capacity all day, only enough to handle the peaks. Flexible staff, cross-training and prep that can wait let you keep a buffer without paying for empty hours.

cards.title: Now it's a software implementation firm.
body: Your firm sets up business software for clients. All six consultants are booked 100%. New clients start together once a month. Launches keep slipping, and every urgent bug derails someone's week.
What do you change?

options.text: Keep everyone fully booked and add a waitlist for new clients
options.feedback: Every billable hour is used, but at full load each surprise turns into a long delay. That's the utilization trap again.

options.text: Leave about a fifth of hours unbooked and start new clients every week
options.feedback: Unbooked hours absorb urgent bugs, and weekly starts shrink the batch so no client waits up to a month. Both concepts at once.

options.text: Start new clients weekly but keep everyone fully booked
options.feedback: Smaller batches cut the wait to start, but with no slack, launches still slip whenever something breaks.

cards.title: Fast service needs small batches and spare capacity.
body: You used two ideas from this unit: **batch size**, because grouping work makes each item wait for the rest, and **the utilization trap**, because waits explode as a team nears 100% busy.
**Try it today:** find one task you save up and do in a batch. Ask what it would take to do it as it arrives.
